back2basics.text: Multilevel climate governance refers to the coordination and cooperation among different levels of government—local, regional, national, and international—to effectively address climate change. Cities play a crucial role as they are centers of population, economic activity, and emissions, and can implement localized climate actions that contribute to national and global goals. Integrating local priorities with national commitments ensures more effective and inclusive climate policies.

2026-10-29-pm-37b0da4a48.deck: The ARISE Cities Forum 2026 in New Delhi adopted the Delhi Declaration on Local Action for Global Climate Goals, calling for enhanced multilevel collaboration of cities in global climate governance ahead of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. This is important for UPSC aspirants to understand India's role in climate diplomacy and the emphasis on urban local bodies in climate action.

editor.mainsAngle: Climate change policy and international cooperation.

body.label: Adoption and purpose
body.text: The Delhi Declaration on Local Action for Global Climate Goals was adopted at the ARISE Cities Forum 2026 to emphasize the role of cities from the Global South in global climate governance and to carry urban priorities to COP31.

body.label: Forum details
body.text: The Forum was held on 27-28 October 2026 at the India Habitat Centre, organised by ICLEI South Asia and NIUA, supported by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, with over 200 participants from 50+ cities across 18+ countries.

body.label: Theme and call
body.text: The Forum's theme was 'From Bharat to Antalya — Commit. Implement. Deliver,' calling for stronger multilevel collaboration and recognition of cities as indispensable partners in climate action.

sections.heading: What is the Delhi Declaration 2026 and its significance?

body.label: Ten shared commitments
body.text: The Declaration sets out ten commitments including advancing the global climate agenda, accelerating adaptation, promoting circularity, achieving energy transition aligned with 1.5°C, prioritising just transitions, institutionalising multilevel climate finance, upholding science and data, creating joint multilevel action spaces, championing Global South urban leadership, and strengthening youth and community leadership.

body.label: Focus on integrated local action
body.text: It stresses integrated local action, just clean energy transition, accessible finance, and meaningful community participation as priorities for effective climate governance.

body.label: Link to COP31
body.text: The Declaration will be presented at COP31 in Antalya, reinforcing that global climate goals require integrating local priorities and implementation capacities into decision-making.

sections.heading: What are the key commitments of the Delhi Declaration 2026?

body.label: Cities as key climate actors
body.text: The Declaration positions cities as key contributors to international climate negotiations, highlighting the need for localizing Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and closing the gap between national commitments and local implementation.

body.label: Multilevel governance emphasis
body.text: It calls for cooperation among all government levels to meet Paris Agreement targets, addressing urban challenges like heat, water stress, infrastructure, and mobility.

body.label: India's climate diplomacy
body.text: India's approach, reflected in the Declaration, aligns with the philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and promotes collaboration, sustainability, resilience, and equity in climate action.

sections.heading: Why does the Delhi Declaration matter for climate governance and India?

body.label: Delhi's urban initiatives
body.text: Delhi has promoted public transport, expanded electric bus fleets, and improved last-mile connectivity with support from ICLEI South Asia to improve air quality.

body.label: Community and leadership roles
body.text: The Declaration highlights the importance of emotional connection to cities, youth and community leadership, and the need for local leaders to have finance and partnerships to act effectively.

body.label: Launch of biodiversity map
body.text: The Forum also launched the Delhi Biodiversity Map developed by ICLEI South Asia, marking a step towards integrating biodiversity in urban climate action.

sections.heading: How does the Forum reflect practical climate action in cities?

back2basics.text: Government securities are debt instruments issued by the government to borrow money from the public. An underwriting auction involves Primary Dealers committing to buy a minimum amount of these securities, ensuring the government can raise the required funds. The Reserve Bank of India facilitates this process, which affects liquidity and interest rates in the economy.

body.label: Definition
body.text: An underwriting auction is a process where Primary Dealers (PDs) commit to buying a minimum amount of government securities, ensuring the government raises the required funds.

body.label: Auction details
body.text: The auction for ₹33,000 crore government securities will be conducted using a multiple price-based method on October 30, 2026.

body.label: Role of Primary Dealers
body.text: Each Primary Dealer has a Minimum Underwriting Commitment (MUC) and a minimum bidding commitment under Additional Competitive Underwriting (ACU) auction, ensuring participation and liquidity.

sections.heading: What is the underwriting auction of Government Securities?

body.label: Securities and notified amounts
body.text: The auction includes four securities: 6.20% GS 2029 (₹9,000 crore), 6.57% GS 2033 (₹12,000 crore), 7.63% GS 2056 (₹9,000 crore), and 7.50% GOI SGrB 2056 (₹3,000 crore).

body.label: Minimum Underwriting Commitment
body.text: For example, each PD must underwrite ₹215 crore for 6.20% GS 2029 and ₹286 crore for 6.57% GS 2033, ensuring minimum participation.

body.label: Bidding process
body.text: PDs submit bids electronically via RBI’s e-Kuber system between 9:00 AM and 9:30 AM on auction day.

sections.heading: Which Government Securities are involved and their commitments?

body.label: Government borrowing
body.text: The auction reflects how the government raises funds to meet its fiscal needs, a key aspect of resource mobilisation.

body.label: Monetary policy instrument
body.text: Government securities auctions influence liquidity and interest rates, impacting monetary policy implementation.

body.label: Exam relevance
body.text: Understanding such auctions helps answer questions on fiscal policy, government budgeting, and the role of RBI in managing public debt.

back2basics.concept: Green Hydrogen and Clean Energy Transition
back2basics.text: Green hydrogen is hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water using renewable energy sources like solar and wind, resulting in low carbon emissions. It serves as an energy carrier that can replace fossil fuels in sectors where direct electrification is difficult. The clean energy transition involves shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy and low-carbon technologies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and combat climate change.

2026-10-29-pm-58652e71ce.deck: Indian companies have signed green hydrogen offtake commitments exceeding 5.5 lakh metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) as of October 2026, positioning India as the global leader in this sector. This development is crucial for UPSC aspirants to understand India's clean energy transition, industrial decarbonisation, and international energy partnerships.

body.label: Definition and production
body.text: Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity, resulting in minimal emissions compared to fossil-based hydrogen production.

body.label: Environmental benefits
body.text: It emits no carbon dioxide when used, helping reduce emissions in hard-to-abate sectors like fertiliser production, petroleum refining, steel manufacturing, heavy transport, and shipping.

body.label: India's resource advantage
body.text: India's abundant solar and wind resources make domestic green hydrogen production feasible, supporting energy security and net-zero emission goals.

sections.heading: What is green hydrogen and why is it important?

body.label: Offtake volume
body.text: Indian companies have signed green hydrogen offtake agreements exceeding 5.5 lakh MTPA as of October 2026, accounting for about 11% of the National Green Hydrogen Mission's target.

body.label: Export orientation
body.text: Over 70% of these commitments are earmarked for exports, strengthening India's position in global markets such as Europe, Japan, South Korea, and Germany.

body.label: Investment scale
body.text: These projects are expected to attract investments of around ₹90,000 crore (approximately USD 9.5 billion), indicating large-scale economic and industrial impact.

sections.heading: What are India's green hydrogen offtake commitments and their significance?

body.label: Mission objectives
body.text: Launched in 2023 with an outlay of ₹19,744 crore, the Mission aims to produce at least 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030.

body.label: Strategic interventions
body.text: The SIGHT programme incentivises domestic electrolyser manufacturing and green hydrogen production, with 15 companies awarded capacity for 3,000 MW electrolyser manufacturing and 8,62,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen production.

body.label: Pilot projects and hubs
body.text: Pilot projects in steel, mobility, and shipping sectors test technology and infrastructure, while designated hydrogen hubs and innovation clusters improve project viability and economies of scale.

body.label: Policy and standards
body.text: The Mission includes waivers on interstate transmission charges, open access to renewable electricity, and India's Green Hydrogen Standard limiting emissions to 2 kg CO₂ equivalent per kg hydrogen.

sections.heading: How is the National Green Hydrogen Mission supporting this growth?

body.label: Major agreements
body.text: Notable contracts include ACME Group's supply of 4,88,000 MTPA green ammonia to Japan, Reliance Industries' $3 billion green ammonia deal with South Korea, and AM Green's agreements with Germany and Japan.

body.label: Export markets
body.text: India supplies green ammonia and methanol to European and Japanese markets, emerging as a competitive global supplier with clean bunkering fuels for shipping.

back2basics.text: Judicial autonomy means that courts and tribunals operate independently without undue influence from the executive branch. Tribunals like the NCLT and NCLAT resolve specialized disputes and require adequate infrastructure and staffing to function efficiently. Maintaining appointment powers within the tribunal preserves this autonomy and ensures accountability.

2026-10-29-pm-627380be37.deck: The Supreme Court expressed concern over the Ministry of Corporate Affairs controlling staff appointments at the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and directed the tribunal presidents to submit proposals on infrastructure and staffing. back2basics.concept: Cyclones and Disaster Management in India
back2basics.text: A cyclone is a large-scale air mass that rotates around a strong center of low atmospheric pressure, often causing heavy rains and strong winds. India’s eastern coast is vulnerable to cyclones originating in the Bay of Bengal. Disaster management involves preparedness, timely evacuation, rescue operations by agencies like NDRF and SDRF, and coordination between central and state governments to reduce loss of life and property.

2026-10-29-pm-8d3f1c1903.deck: Cyclone Arnab, a very severe cyclonic storm, made landfall near the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28, 2026, causing heavy rains, strong winds, and disruption in multiple states. The Union Home Minister assured full central assistance, with rescue operations underway and impact assessments planned, highlighting disaster management and inter-state coordination.

body.label: Cyclone classification
body.text: Cyclone Arnab was classified as a 'very severe cyclonic storm' with maximum sustained winds of 125-135 kmph gusting to 150 kmph.

body.label: Landfall location and timing
body.text: The cyclone made landfall near the Andhra Pradesh coast between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, close to south of Yanam, starting around 1:20 a.m. on October 28, 2026.

body.label: Movement and impact area
body.text: The cyclone moved at 18-23 kmph, with its northern spiral band entering land and affecting coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha.

sections.heading: What was the nature and path of Cyclone Arnab?

body.label: Central government coordination
body.text: Union Home Minister Amit Shah spoke with Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh, assuring full assistance and deploying NDRF and SDRF teams for rescue and relief.

body.label: State-level preparedness
body.text: Andhra Pradesh evacuated about 89,000 people from coastal areas, set up cyclone shelters, and mobilized sanitation and road-clearing teams; Odisha deployed 60 teams of ODRAF and put police on high alert.

body.label: Impact mitigation measures
body.text: Authorities warned of severe waterlogging, power outages, and falling trees; flights and trains were cancelled to ensure safety; fishermen were advised to stay ashore.

sections.heading: How did the states and central government respond to Cyclone Arnab?

body.label: Rainfall and wind damage
body.text: Visakhapatnam recorded over 100 mm of rain in a day, with 206 trees uprooted and roads blocked; heavy rains caused flooding and power cuts in multiple districts.

body.label: Casualties and safety issues
body.text: One man died after coming into contact with a snapped live wire in Visakhapatnam; reluctance to evacuate was noted in Yanam despite warnings.

body.label: Transport disruptions
body.text: Numerous flights were cancelled at Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam airports, and train services were affected in Telangana and neighboring states.

body.label: Scheme overview
body.text: PMEGP is a flagship credit-linked subsidy programme by the Ministry of MSME aimed at creating sustainable self-employment through new micro-enterprises in the non-farm sector.

body.label: Implementation
body.text: The scheme is implemented nationally by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) with support from agencies like KVIBs, District Industries Centres, and Coir Board.

body.label: Financial assistance
body.text: Entrepreneurs receive margin money subsidy on bank-sanctioned project loans to set up micro-enterprises, along with awareness, capacity building, market linkages, and post-establishment support.

body.label: Employment generation
body.text: These enterprises are expected to generate over 1.02 lakh sustainable employment opportunities, mainly in rural areas.

body.label: Inclusive focus
body.text: The assistance targets women-led entrepreneurship, SC/ST communities, and focuses on North Eastern Region and Aspirational Districts for balanced regional development.

body.label: Performance since 2014-15
body.text: Since FY 2014-15, PMEGP has facilitated over 8.38 lakh micro enterprises with bank loans exceeding ₹70,000 crore and margin money subsidy over ₹25,193 crore, generating about 75 lakh jobs.

sections.heading: What are the recent developments and impact of PMEGP?

body.label: Rural and social inclusion
body.text: Nearly 80% of assisted units are in rural areas, with about 50% beneficiaries from SC, ST, and OBC categories, and 40% enterprises owned by women entrepreneurs.

body.label: Entrepreneurship and local economies
body.text: PMEGP promotes grassroots entrepreneurship, strengthens local economies, and supports sustainable livelihoods, aligning with the government's vision of an inclusive, self-reliant economy.

back2basics.text: The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) is a constitutional authority responsible for administering elections in India. back2basics.text: Minimum Support Price is a government-set price at which it purchases crops from farmers to ensure they receive a minimum profit margin over production costs. It acts as a safety net against price volatility in agricultural markets, encouraging farmers to invest in production and secure stable incomes. MSP is announced annually for mandated crops based on cost and market factors.

body.label: Price assurance mechanism
body.text: MSP provides a guaranteed price to farmers for eligible crops, protecting them from adverse market price fluctuations and ensuring remunerative returns.

body.label: Supports agricultural planning
body.text: By assuring minimum returns, MSP encourages farmers to invest in improved seeds, technology, and inputs, aiding informed agricultural decisions.

body.label: Stabilizes farm income
body.text: MSP reduces uncertainty for small and marginal farmers by providing a fallback price when market prices fall below the announced MSP.

sections.heading: What is the Minimum Support Price and why is it important?

body.label: CACP recommendations
body.text: MSPs are based on the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices' recommendations considering production costs, demand-supply, price parity, and a minimum 50% margin over cost.

body.label: Rabi 2027-28 MSP increases
body.text: MSPs for all mandated Rabi crops were increased, with safflower seeing the highest absolute increase of ₹675 per quintal and wheat having the highest margin over cost at 106%.

body.label: Digital platforms and transparency
body.text: Platforms like e-Samriddhi and e-Samyukti facilitate farmer registration, procurement, and direct payment, enhancing transparency and reducing intermediaries.

body.label: Biometric authentication

body.label: Application window
body.text: The online application portal https://pli.texmin.gov.in will be open from 1st November to 31st December 2026 for new applications under Round 4.

body.label: Eligibility
body.text: Companies with minimum turnover of ₹100 crore under Part 2 category and existing participants who have not claimed incentives can apply or migrate respectively.

body.label: Compliance with guidelines
body.text: Applicants must submit their applications within the stipulated period following the scheme guidelines.
